newsitem.title: USA: Motorola expected to report lower Q4 net.
newsitem.headline: Motorola expected to report lower Q4 net.

text.p: Motorola Inc is expected to report lower earnings for the third consecutive quarter on Thursday, but analysts will be looking for any hints of a rebound in new semiconductor orders and in its wireless phone business.

Motorola said it will release fourth quarter results after the market closes on Thursday. According to First Call, the consensus of analysts' estimates is $0.41 a share, compared with $0.72 a share for the quarter last year.
"I suspect investors are going to be looking harder at new orders, particularly in the semiconductor sector," said Robert Wilkes, an analyst for Brown Brothers Harriman.
Motorola, citing company policy, declined comment on the estimates.

Although fourth quarter earnings are expected to fall some 43 percent from a year ago, analysts said they expect Motorola to meet their earnings expectations for the quarter. Some analysts also expect a stronger second half to make 1997 a better year overall for the company.
"The second half looks much better...I think it's going to become a second-half story," Hambrecht & Quist analyst Rakesh Sood said, adding that the March quarter tends to be seasonally slow.
Motorola's key businesses, its semiconductors and its wireless telephones, have dragged sales lower for the two previous quarters -- the first time since 1985 Motorola has seen sales declines.
"I'm actually looking at revenue declining six percent, at about $6.9 billion" for the fourth quarter, said Monish Bahl, an analyst for Parker/Hunter Inc..
But analysts said they are expecting to see at least an indication of a slight turnaround, especially in semiconductors, which accounted for about 29 percent of Motorola's sales in 1995.
"The semiconductor business seems to have picked up in the end of the year," Wilkes said.
Despite the optimism, analysts agree that Motorola's chip business is still lagging behind the industry as a whole.
The Semiconductor Industry Association said the chip industry's book-to-bill ratio, an indicator of future demand, was 1.15 in November, up from a revised 1.11 in October.
Last quarter Motorola had a book-to-bill ratio of 0.82. Bahl said he is looking for 0.95 to 1.00 for this quarter.
"I think that semiconductors have really bottomed out," Bahl said.

In Motorola's general systems sector, which includes wireless phone handsets which have been hit by stiff competition and pricing pressure, analysts said they also expect to see at least a slight rebound. The sector accounted for about 36 percent of Motorola's sales in 1995.
"They're rolling out some new handsets and may show some improvement," Wilkes said, adding Motorola has launched a new digital phone in Europe and has two others ready for 1997.
Motorola is expected to report a one-time charge related to layoffs last quarter, mainly in the semiconductor sector. When the company reported third quarter earnings, it said to expect the charge.
But analysts said the cutbacks are helping.

Overall, some analysts said they are looking for a more notable turnaround in the second half of 1997, as changes from the new management begin to show up. Christopher Galvin was promoted to chief executive, and the former chief executive Gary Tooker serves as chairman.
"Like any large organization, it takes a while for the changes to take hold," Sood said.
((--Chicago newsdesk, 312-408-8787))
